tier_reason: The thekvs/cpp-serializers README results table, produced by benchmark.cpp and yas/record.cpp, is a widely cited third-party shootout. It shows yas at 302.7 ms against boost at 1195.04 ms and cereal at 1052.46 ms. It gives only 'Intel Core i7', Ubuntu 16.04 and a CMake Release build, with no compiler, so it is not A. The fraillt suite is third-party with respect to yas and states the compiler and -O2 but no CPU model.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: thekvs suite: C++14, cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; the compiler for the published table is not stated (the README only says it was 'tested with Clang and GCC'). fraillt suite: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1; CMakeLists.txt appends -O2 and defines NDEBUG with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20 (the README/CI cmake call passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE).
corrections.caveats: The yas README says yas was created 'as a replacement of boost.serialization because of its insufficient speed' and cites both suites. Both suites are third-party with respect to yas: thekvs, and fraillt, who is the author of the competing library bitsery. Neither names an exact CPU model and thekvs does not name the compiler, so the evidence is not tier A. The win belongs to yas's default binary archive. In thekvs, 'yas-compact' (2063.34 ms) is slower than boost (1195.04) and cereal (1052.46). In fraillt, the std::stringstream-backed 'yas stream' case (GCC 10871/11182 ms) is no faster than cereal (10777/9088). Both runs are old: thekvs used yas 7.0.2 and boost 1.69 (repo last touched 2019); fraillt used yas 7.1.0, boost 1.77 and cereal 1.3.0. The repo has no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no license, but every sampled header under include/yas carries the Boost Software License 1.0 text.

notes: All claimed numbers appear verbatim: the thekvs table and the GCC 11 table in fraillt. The ratios check out (6.6x/7.2x vs boost, 4.7x/5.1x vs cereal). License fixed: all 13 sampled headers, including include/yas/serialize.hpp, carry the BSL-1.0 notice, so usability changes to copyable. The last commit (2025-02-18) is confirmed, so the status stays stale.

tier_reason: This is a first-party suite: fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark is by bitsery's author, with code in bitsery/bitsery.cpp, boost/boost.cpp, cereal/cereal.cpp and testing_core/. It states the compiler (GCC 11 / Clang 12.0.1) and flags (-O2 -DNDEBUG in CMakeLists.txt) but no CPU model. That rules out A, and being first-party rules out B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark README, 'general' test case. GCC 11: bitsery 1470 ms ser / 1524 ms des vs boost 15126/12724 ms (~10.3x/~8.3x) and cereal 10777/9088 ms (~7.3x/~6.0x). Clang 12.0.1: bitsery 2128/1832 ms vs boost 16011/13017 ms (~7.5x/~7.1x) and cereal 9977/8565 ms (~4.7x/~4.7x). Ratios derived from page data. bitsery's own README shows an older GCC 10.3.0 run: bitsery 1119/1166 ms vs boost 15391/12912 ms and cereal 10518/10245 ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1. CMakeLists.txt appends -O2, defines NDEBUG, MONSTERS=50 and SAMPLES=300000, and sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20. The README/CI cmake call passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (the CI job names say 'Release').
corrections.workload: Serialize/deserialize a vector of 50 randomly generated nested 'Monster' structs (fixed seed; vectors, strings, enums, weapons) 300,000 times after 5 warmup rounds, on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 with GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 (fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark suite)
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party comparison: the benchmark repo belongs to bitsery's author (fraillt). The compiler and -O2 are stated but the CPU model is not, so the tier is C. The headline numbers in bitsery's README (1119/1166 ms, GCC 10.3.0) come from an older run than the GCC 11 / Clang 12 tables in the benchmark repo. bitsery's lead shrinks under Clang (~4.7x vs cereal). zpp_bits beats bitsery on the same page (GCC 733/693 ms). The page itself notes that the protobuf and flatbuffers comparisons are not fully fair because of conversion to the custom types.

notes: The claim mixed two runs. The 1119/1166 ms figures come from bitsery's README (GCC 10.3.0, different boost/cereal numbers), and the 1524/1561 ms figures on the benchmark page are deserialize times, not serialize times. So '~10-14x vs boost' and '~7-9x vs cereal' overstated the benchmark_url data, which shows ~7.1-10.3x and ~4.7-7.3x for the 'general' case. last_commit corrected to 2025-10-08 (the push was 2025-10-09). The status stays 'active' but passes the 12-month mark in mid-October 2026. The page tables match the repo's GitHub Actions ubuntu-20.04 matrix, so they may come from CI runners, but I could not confirm that; hardware is left as is.

tier_reason: This is first-party: chronoxor wrote both FBE and CppSerialization. The benchmark code is public (performance/fbe_serialize.cpp, protobuf_serialize.cpp and the others), and the CppBenchmark reports give the CPU (Apple M1 Pro) and 'Process configuration: release' but no compiler or flags. That rules out A, and being first-party rules out B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: CppSerialization README (CppBenchmark, Apple M1 Pro, run 2025-07-16): FBE 77 ns serialize / 84 ns deserialize vs Protobuf 322/351 ns (~4.2x/~4.2x, derived from page data). FBE is also faster than Cap'n Proto (247/184 ns) and than FlatBuffers at serialization (272 ns). FlatBuffers deserializes in 81 ns vs FBE's 84 ns, and SimpleBinaryEncoding (35/52 ns) and zpp::bits (34/37 ns) beat FBE on the same page.
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 Pro (CppBenchmark reports 10 cores at 2.400 GHz), 32 GiB RAM, OS version 24.5.0 (Darwin), run 2025-07-16
corrections.workload: CppBenchmark fixtures (performance/*_serialize.cpp, *_deserialize.cpp): serialize/deserialize one Account with a wallet and three Orders (128-byte domain object; 120-280-byte messages depending on format), 5 attempts of 5 s each. The Protobuf path builds a fresh message and converts from the domain model on each operation.
corrections.caveats: This is first-party: FastBinaryEncoding and the comparison repo CppSerialization share the author (chronoxor). The CppBenchmark reports state the CPU (Apple M1 Pro) and 'release' but not the compiler or flags, so the tier is C. The table in FBE's own README (FBE 66/82 ns vs Protobuf 628/759 ns) is a stale 2018 run on an Intel Core i7-6700K / Windows 8 and does not match the current CppSerialization page. The Protobuf benchmark allocates a new message and converts from the domain model on every operation, with no arena. FBE is not the fastest on its own page: SimpleBinaryEncoding and zpp::bits are ~2x faster, and FlatBuffers deserialization is about even (81 vs 84 ns).

notes: The record's numbers (66/82, 628/759, 558/359, 830/290 ns) are not on benchmark_url. They come from a 2018 Intel i7-6700K / Windows 8 run that is still shown in FBE's README and was on the CppSerialization README until the July 2025 refresh (I checked README at commit cea1bee5bb). The record paired those old numbers with the current M1 Pro hardware. On the current page the gain over Protobuf is ~4.2x rather than ~9.5x, and the claim that FBE also beats FlatBuffers does not hold for deserialization. License (MIT), stars (961) and last commit (2026-09-10) are confirmed.
